answer: Every quartz crystal keeps its own time: no two oscillators tick alike. Kohno proved in 2005: a machine's clock skew, read from TCP timestamps, fingerprints it across the ocean. Each ballot enrolls its skew over one hour, then must spiral within 0.5 ppm of its line across 40 probes a tide. One rack running 10,000 ballots on a single crystal shows 10,000 identical skews, so the whole flock forfeits its $25 bonds, $250,000 gone. Forging 10,000 crystals costs 10,000 machines, $500,000 in hardware — like shells on a beach, no two clocks wash up alike, and a copied tick is a dead ballot.
